papers.title: Mapping long-distance jump dispersal risk by leveraging transport infrastructure data and sampling bias correction: a case study with the invasive spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula)
papers.authors: Joseph A. Keller, Nadège Bélouard, Sebastiano De Bona, Jocelyn E. Behm, Matthew R. Helmus
papers.abstract: Long-distance jump dispersal accelerates invasive species spread. Analysis of past jumps can identify invasion pathways and point to locations at risk of future colonization, but spatial bias in survey records obscures patterns. To inform surveillance for the spreading invasive grape pest Lycorma delicatula (Hemiptera: Fulgoridae), we gathered 82,890 agency records of established invasive populations from the United States. We used a clustering algorithm to identify 207 jump dispersal sites, and we developed a bias-aware comparison dataset by filtering records to identify proactive search effort at locations not yet known to hold L. delicatula. We measured points' proximity to a co-produced list of 22 property types encompassing categories with high vehicle traffic, railroads, and related contexts that may transport L. delicatula. Bootstrapping analysis showed that proactive surveys were concentrated near hypothesized influential property types, confirming substantial sampling bias. With this bias accounted for, historical jump dispersal sites were closer than expected to 15 property types, particularly distribution centers, truck rentals, flea markets, and importers. papers.title: The ecological adaptability of pinewood nematode populations: survival strategies, mechanisms and co‐evolution
papers.authors: Chen‐Xi Ying, Tong‐Yue Wen, Xiao‐Lei Ding, Xiao‐Qin Wu
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Bursaphelenchus xylophilus (pinewood nematode, PWN) is the causal agent of pine wilt disease and ranks among the most destructive invasive pests threatening global forest ecosystems. Since its introduction to China, this nematode has triggered massive ecological and economic losses, while its distribution range continues to expand northward. The association between the widespread dispersal of B. xylophilus in invaded areas and the ecological adaptability of its populations has drawn considerable attention. RESULTS: This review systematically synthesizes recent research advances regarding the ecological adaptability of PWN populations, elaborating on molecular mechanisms and ecological strategies that enable the nematode to colonize novel environments. In terms of thermal adaptation, differentially expressed genes, small heat shock protein families and the accumulation of key metabolites collectively shape adaptive pathways to resist extreme high and low temperature stress. For host adaptation, PWN displays polyphagous feeding habits and relies on diverse arboreal fungi as nutritional resources when pines were weakened or died. papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Reveals Spatial Strategies for Slowing Biological Invasions
papers.authors: Jean-Nicolas Lang, Adam Lampert
papers.abstract: Managing biological invasions requires deciding where, when, and how to act while populations continue to grow and spread. Invasive species threaten ecosystems and livelihoods, but limited management resources mean that managers cannot treat every affected area. This study asks how control efforts can be directed across a landscape to slow an invasion while keeping costs low. We develop a reinforcement-learning framework that can use broader spatial context to control biological invasions, using the spongy moth as a case study. The stochastic simulator captures host-dependent growth, short- and long-distance dispersal, density-dependent mating, and the effects of multiple treatments. The reinforcement-learning strategies are compared with benchmarks that are based on local treatment rules. We find that reinforcement learning achieves the lowest mean cost, with its advantage widening as management complexity increases, such as with simultaneous advancing-front control, nascent-colony management, and established-colony containment on heterogeneous-host landscapes. papers.title: Y-linked Genome Editor (YLE) a Self-Limiting Genetic Control Tool: An Updated Review
papers.authors: Poornima R., Mahalakshmi B.R., Shruthi D.J., Rajesha S., Kiran Kumar H.B.
papers.source: OpenAlex / International Journal of Environmental and Agriculture Research
papers.abstract: Invasive species are increasingly impacting forests, food, fisheries, and agriculture, with global economic repercussions. The majority of vertebrate pest management methods lack effective strategic control tools and are unsustainable and unsuitable for effective landscape-scale management. The application of genetic techniques is intended to prevent invasive populations. Employment of a mix of strategies has enabled sustained control, depending on the species, region, and degree of dissemination. Advantages of the genetic methods include species specificity, long-term and self-sustainability, 100% trait transferability, minimum infrastructure requirement, and non-requirement of physical modification of the landscape. This renders these methods feasible and applicable globally to control a large number of invasive pests. The possibility of using gene drive technology in conjunction with conventional control techniques opens new horizons in the management of vertebrate invasive populations. papers.title: Proposal for monitoring the Eastern Grey Squirrel (Sciurus carolinensis) in Poland
papers.authors: Barbara Kominek, Joanna Gruszczyńska
papers.abstract: The report presents a nationwide, continuous monitoring program for the invasive eastern grey squirrel (Sciurus carolinensis) in Poland, aimed at early detection and prevention of its spread. Monitoring focuses on high-risk areas such as urban parks, deciduous forests near cities, protected areas and border regions. The program includes repeated surveys across seasons using camera traps, field observations, winter nest searches and citizen reports. Grey squirrels pose a serious threat to native fauna, particularly the red squirrel, through competition and disease transmission. Immediate removal of detected individuals, strict enforcement of legal bans, cross-border cooperation and public awareness are emphasized. Effective monitoring combined with rapid response offers a real opportunity to prevent the establishment of this invasive species in Poland.

papers.authors: Xiaoxue Ma, Hanqi Xie, Qunfang Huang, Yang E. Hong, Jinmeng Zhang
papers.abstract: The invasion and spread of alien aquatic organisms pose an increasing threat to ecosystem stability and functioning, biodiversity conservation, and socioeconomic development under ongoing climate change. However, limited attention has been given to the compound ecological risks of multi-species invasions driven by the combined effects of climate factors, topography, water quality, vegetation, and other environmental variables under future climate scenarios. Focusing on Pomacea canaliculata (P. canaliculata) and Pontederia crassipes ( P. crassipes ), this study employed the MaxEnt model and spatial analysis to identify key environmental determinants and to project current and future habitat suitability in the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River Basin under SSP245 and SSP585 scenarios. The results show that the MaxEnt model performed with high accuracy for P. crassipes (AUC = 0.954) and good accuracy for P. canaliculata (AUC = 0.880). papers.title: Restoration decisions in highly variable systems: Whether, when, and how to enhance kelp
papers.authors: Mei Z. Blundell, Marissa L. Baskett
papers.abstract: In highly variable ecosystems, natural variability can obscure signals of decline that warrant intervention, as there is often a lack of long-term data needed to distinguish between declines that are transient and likely to recover naturally and those that would be permanent without intervention. Implementing restoration for a species involves deciding on a threshold condition at which to intervene, duration that this threshold needs to be met before intervening, life stages at introduction, and amounts to introduce. Current bull and giant kelp restoration efforts in California were spurred by persistent kelp loss that started in 2013 following a disease outbreak among predators of the primary herbivore and a marine heatwave. We asked how decisions about intervention cue, threshold, wait time, life stage at introduction, and amount affect population outcomes against a backdrop of environmental variability. We analyzed additional context-dependencies on grazing and climate intensity. papers.title: Primary and secondary invasion pathways: why the distinction matters
papers.authors: Susan Canavan, Julian D. Avery, Jacob N. Barney, Evelyn M. Beaury, Kim Canavan
papers.abstract: Abstract The pathways by which non-native species are introduced and spread shape the rate and geographic patterns of biological invasions. They can be classified as primary, where species cross jurisdictional or biogeographic boundaries, or secondary, where they move within those boundaries after introduction. Despite economic, political, social, and ecological differences between these pathway types, most classification schemes and regulatory frameworks do not explicitly distinguish between them. Primary pathways are relatively well-defined and subject to biosecurity regulation, while secondary pathways remain poorly characterized and largely overlooked in policy and practice. Secondary pathways create multiple nodes from which species spread, complicating containment. Here we refine the distinction between primary and secondary pathways and explore how failing to recognize this distinction can limit the effectiveness of biosecurity systems, particularly by leaving secondary pathways inadequately addressed. papers.title: Prevention of Destructive Fishing in the Waters of Tual City: Effective Surveillance and Law Enforcement Strategies
papers.authors: Suharta ., Sigit Bintoro, Riyan Maulana, Ismi Isti Anah
papers.source: Crossref / International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research and Growth Evaluation
papers.abstract: <jats:p>Destructive fishing in the waters of Tual City remains a significant environmental and socio-economic issue, threatening marine biodiversity and the livelihoods of local fishermen. This study analyzes the problem using a SWOT approach, identifying strengths such as existing government regulations and rich marine resources, weaknesses including limited enforcement capacity and economic dependence on harmful fishing practices, opportunities such as growing global demand for sustainable seafood, and threats like illegal fishing and climate change. Based on the SWOT analysis, several policy recommendations are proposed, including strengthening law enforcement, promoting sustainable alternative livelihoods, enhancing education and awareness programs, expanding marine protected areas (MPAs), and creating market incentives for responsible fisheries. These strategies aim to transition Tual City towards sustainable fisheries management, balancing environmental conservation with economic development. Effective implementation of these policies will not only mitigate destructive fishing but also ensure long-term resilience for both the ecosystem and local fishing communities.</jats:p>

papers.abstract: Campylobacter is a constant concern in ensuring food safety, as it is one of the most common pathogens in food. The main source of Campylobacter species in food is poultry meat, and the primary production of this meat is a critical point where measures need to be taken to reduce its presence in the food chain. Therefore, poultry slaughterhouses are recognized as places where it is necessary to implement measures to control and reduce the number of Campylobacter spp. Food business operators are obliged to ensure greater hygiene on the slaughter line, through the inspection of equipment for each step of slaughter and the application of regular cleaning protocols. Continuous monitoring of the presence and abundance of Campylobacter spp. on the slaughter line provides data on the validity of hygiene control measures in the slaughterhouse, as well as the data needed to assess the microbiological risk in poultry meat. papers.title: Could local climate, forest site and stand conditions mitigate the defoliation in European beech stands? – The case of southern Belgium
papers.authors: Marie-Pierre Tasseroul, Philippe Lejeune, Yves Brostaux, Adrien Michez, Hugues Titeux
papers.abstract: Although climate change has been a major factor in the declining health of European beech (Fagus sylvatica L.) stands since the end of the 20th century, it seems that local site and stand conditions may play a key role within the beech’s climax region by exacerbating or mitigating this phenomenon. In this study, we assessed crown defoliation in 1,515 dominant trees distributed across 101 mature beech stands, located along bioclimatic and ecological gradients in the Ardenne region (southern Belgium) during July and August 2022. A large dataset covering past and present climate, local forest site and stand conditions was analysed using a Random Forest model, combined with a variable selection (VSURF) and interpretated by the Shapley values method. The final model explained 45% of the observed variability in stand defoliation and identified five key drivers. Warmer spring conditions and moderate increases in temperature during the growing season were associated with reduced crown damages, reflecting climate conditions that remained suitable to beech. papers.abstract: Aquatic species of economic and ecological importance are increasingly threatened by environmental change, yet their genetic diversity and population structure remain poorly characterised, limiting effective conservation and management. To address this gap, we initiated a multi-species genomic monitoring programme in 2022, targeting key marine and freshwater taxa. A total of 2,420 individuals from 104 locations were sampled across six species: turbot (Scophthalmus maximus), zander (Sander lucioperca), European eel (Anguilla anguilla; both glass eel in the marine environment and adult eel in freshwater environments), blue mussel (Mytilus edulis), flat oyster (Ostrea edulis), and Pacific oyster (Magallana gigas). Using genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS) and SNP arrays, we generated genome-wide SNP datasets to assess population structure, genetic diversity, inbreeding, and relatedness. papers.abstract: Wild boar (Sus scrofa) is one of the most widely distributed wild ungulates, and its populations are increasing and expanding globally due to socioeconomic change, reduced predator pressure, and climate warming. Rooting, a characteristic foraging behavior in which wild boars overturn litter, vegetation, and soil, is a major disturbance in forest ecosystems and can alter soil properties, biotic communities, ecosystem processes, and ecosystem services. In this literature review, we synthesize current knowledge of wild boar rooting in forest ecosystems. We first summarize the drivers of rooting regimes. papers.abstract: Hypoxia is closely associated with tumor progression, metastasis, therapeutic resistance, and diagnostic challenges. The timely detection of hypoxia in live cancer cells is critical for early cancer diagnosis and for monitoring the effectiveness of anticancer therapies. Recently, there has been growing interest in non-covalent supramolecular design strategies for the development of hypoxia-sensitive sensors and prodrugs. Unlike the widely employed covalent approach, supramolecular chemistry eliminates the need for complex and time-consuming synthetic processes. Instead, the individual components of the sensor autonomously self-assemble into the desired structure. This review provides an overview of hypoxia-targeted and hypoxia-activated supramolecular probes, along with their mechanisms of action in tumor diagnosis and therapy. The supramolecular systems considered are classified according to the use of certain classes of macrocycles. The role of macrocyclic derivatives in the various proposed approaches and the response patterns of hypoxic targets will also be analyzed. papers.title: Spontaneous neuropathic pain
papers.authors: Xiangsunze Zeng, Clifford J. Woolf
papers.abstract: Spontaneous pain is a highly prevalent and disabling consequence of neuropathic disorders, yet it remains mechanistically underdefined and therapeutically underserved. Historically, preclinical animal models and clinical trials have been overwhelmingly biased toward stimulus-evoked hypersensitivity, relegating spontaneous pain to a secondary manifestation. Emerging evidence now challenges this view. Converging data from pharmacology, neural recordings, and systems-level causal manipulations indicate that spontaneous and stimulus-evoked pain arise from substantially dissociable molecular, cellular, and circuit substrates. Injured-fiber–derived ectopic activity within specific sensory neuron subtypes serves as a dominant peripheral generator of spontaneous pain, whereas cellularly distinct, intact spared-fiber pathways mediate stimulus-evoked hypersensitivity. At spinal and supraspinal levels, spontaneous pain preferentially engages affective–salience networks during pain chronification and may ultimately become stabilized within higher-order circuitry—while remaining dynamically coupled to afferent input. In the first study, we examined the actigraphic profiles of individuals without a psychiatric diagnosis who were characterised by cyclothymic temperament (CFG) or positive schizotypal traits (PSF), compared with controls. papers.abstract: Date palm (Phoenix dactylifera L.) cultivation in the Arabian Peninsula represents a six- millennium agronomic tradition now undergoing rapid genomic and phytochemical reappraisal. This Review synthesises advances across cultivar genomics, salinity tolerance, pest and disease biology, fruit phytochemistry and clinical evidence, while subjecting methodologically contested domains to critical appraisal. papers.authors: Daniel Pires, Cidália Gomes, Belinda Groom, Sylvain Dufour, Emmanuel Danquah
papers.abstract: Abstract The bushmeat trade in Africa is a largely unregulated activity that drives the unsustainable exploitation of wild terrestrial vertebrates—an issue often coined the bushmeat crisis. We build on a four-gene mitochondrial DNA-typing approach to develop an unprecedented reference database framework for effectively tracing the bushmeat trade in tropical Africa. Our dataset comprises over 2,500 samples collected over a 13-yr period across 10 African countries and two European airports. Relying on an expert analytical pipeline and ∼8,700 nucleotide sequences, we identified 96% of samples to the species-level. In contrast, we estimated that conventional two-gene approaches would have yielded 18–26% erroneous or inconclusive taxonomic assignments. DNA-typing refined > 50% of field identifications, with refinement reaching 92-95% for highly processed carcasses seized in Europe. Leveraging expanded taxonomic representation, we empirically refined the genetic species thresholds applied to bushmeat and provide a reproducible pipeline for using our expert reference database from NCBI. papers.abstract: Abstract Rice blast, caused by Magnaporthe oryzae , threatens rice production and is a model for fungal pathogenicity. The Korean rice isolate KJ201 has supported extensive functional, transcriptomic, and epigenomic research, but its fragmented reference genome has limited chromosome-scale interpretation. PacBio HiFi and Hi-C sequencing produced a 44.8 Mb assembly comprising seven chromosome-scale scaffolds and three mini-scaffolds, with an N50 of 6.5 Mb and 98.5% complete BUSCOs. Comparative analysis with 17 public M. oryzae genomes placed KJ201 with the East Asian rice isolates P131 and O-135, apart from the 70 − 15/Guy11 lineage. The seven core chromosomes were broadly conserved, whereas localized chromosome-terminal differences and breakpoint patterns differentiated rice subclades and host-associated groups. Gene-family content was largely conserved. papers.title: Tracking Plum Curculio (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) Movement in Blueberry and Peach Fields Using Protein Immunomarkers
papers.authors: Timothy P Lampasona, Cesar Rodriguez‐Saona, Anne L. Nielsen
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Plum curculio, Conotrachelus nenuphar (Herbst), is a native fruit pest. Adults emerge from overwintering sites in wooded areas and disperse into crop fields in the spring. However, their movement patterns within fields after this initial dispersal remain poorly understood. In this study, we used protein markers to investigate the in‐field dispersal of C. nenuphar adults in peach ( Prunus persica L.) and highbush blueberry ( Vaccinium corymbosum L.) fields. Chicken egg albumin (egg whites) was applied along field borders and bovine casein (cow's milk) within field interiors. Adults were collected daily using beat sampling, and enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) were used to detect egg and/or milk proteins on individual insects. This approach provided a form of behavioural forensics, allowing us to trace each insect's movement within the field. Results indicated a strong edge effect in both crops, with 64.3% and 78.0% of adults collected along the border in blueberry and peach, respectively. papers.title: Instance-Wise Contrastive Graph Neural Network Enables the Discovery of Novel Aedes aegypti Larvicidal Compounds
papers.authors: Karine Santana Lúcio da Costa, Gustavo Henrique Garcia Caldeira, Vinícius Alexandre Fiaia Costa, Amanda Santana Silva, Carolina da Silva Pereira

papers.abstract: Abstract Aedes aegypti remains a major arboviral vector, making larval control a critical strategy to reduce mosquito populations. However, resistance to commercial larvicides has reduced the long-term effectiveness of current interventions, reinforcing the need for new compounds with improved potency and selectivity. Here, we present an instance-wise contrastive graph neural network (GNN) framework to accelerate the discovery of novel larvicidal compounds. The model was trained on a curated dataset of 556 organic compounds organized into LC 50 -derived multitask classification thresholds and integrated Transformer-inspired graph learning with whole-molecule and fragment-level contrastive regularization. This model achieved strong held-out performance, with global AUC = 0.95 ± 0.01, PR-AUC = 0.93 ± 0.01, and MCC = 0.77 ± 0.03, outperforming conventional machine learning and graph-based baselines. Predictive uncertainty analysis and counterfactual maps further supported the interpretation of threshold-sensitive predictions and substructural contribution patterns. papers.title: Optimal Control Analysis and Cost‐Effectiveness Calculations of Chickenpox Transmission Dynamics

papers.source: OpenAlex / Optimal Control Applications and Methods
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study develops and analyses a mathematical model for chickenpox transmission dynamics. The model's basic properties, including positivity, boundedness, and stability of disease‐free and endemic equilibria, are rigorously established. The basic reproduction number is derived, and sensitivity analysis identifies the most sensitive parameters. An optimal control problem is formulated with four time‐dependent controls (preventive measures, vaccination, pharmaceutical interventions, and non‐pharmaceutical treatments). Numerical simulations using a forward‐backward sweep method (FBSM) are conducted. Several control scenarios that resulted from the intersection of the recommended controls to clarify the impact of these controls and explore the most effective way to halt the disease's progress are presented. Moreover, the cost‐effectiveness analysis is presented to offer a quantitative comparison between the suggested five control scenarios. papers.authors: Yun Xing, Fengxu Chen, Gonggeng Liu, Shijun Bao, Xujian Zhang
papers.abstract: The widespread proliferation of electromagnetic technologies in communications, healthcare, and daily life poses increasing risks of radiation-induced tissue injury. Mitigating these deleterious effects remains a formidable challenge. Recently, medical gases, including molecular hydrogen (H2), hydrogen sulfide (H2S), carbon monoxide (CO), nitric oxide (NO), and hyperbaric oxygen, have emerged as a promising therapeutic modality with radioprotective potential. These gases exert their effects through integrated, anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, and mitochondrial-protective mechanisms. Specifically, the endogenous gasotransmitters (CO, NO, and H2S) modulate precise signaling networks, while the exogenous interventions (H2, and hyperbaric oxygen) function primarily through direct radical scavenging or the induction of hormetic stress responses. This review evaluates the research progress of these five medical gases in preventing and treating injuries across the electromagnetic spectrum. H2 possesses the broadest evidence base, particularly in radiofrequency and ultraviolet protection. H2S and CO demonstrate potent efficacy in addressing ultraviolet-induced skin and retinal damage. papers.abstract: The ability of the rhizosphere to recruit beneficial microorganisms is central to the sustainable management of crops. Here, we investigated, through shotgun metagenomic sequencing and mass spectrometry techniques, the microbial composition, antimicrobial resistance (AMRs), and metabolomic profiles of Piper nigrum cultivated under two support systems: living Gliricidia sepium support (SL/RL) and dead wooden support (SD/RD). Bulk and rhizosphere soils were sequenced to assess taxonomic structure and ARGs, with emphasis on Actinobacteria due to their relevance in antibiotic production. Actinobacteria were highly represented across the samples (~ 35%). papers.source: OpenAlex / International Journal of Environmental and Agriculture Research
papers.abstract: Wilt caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cucumerinum is a serious soil-borne disease of cucumber (Cucumis sativus L.) that causes major yield losses, particularly under continuous cultivation. A survey conducted in the Coimbatore region during 2024–2025 revealed wide variation in wilt incidence across locations, ranging from 4.70 to 80.13%. Four integrated disease management (IDM) modules were evaluated under field conditions during 2025 and 2026. Among them, Module 2, comprising soil application and seed treatment with a Trichoderma asperellum + Bacillus subtilis consortium and soil drenching with B. subtilis along with clove oil EC formulation (0.1%), recorded the lowest wilt incidence and the highest yield in both years. Pooled analysis confirmed Module 2 as the best treatment (11.60% wilt incidence, 9.20 t/ha yield and B:C ratio of 2.90) compared with 47.30% wilt incidence and 5.90 t/ha yield in the untreated control. papers.authors: Corinne Manuela Gerber, Giulia Zezza, Valeria Guidi, Michele Wyler, Claudia Bachofen
papers.abstract: Switzerland hosts over 400 bird species, many of which are migratory. Through diverse movement patterns, ranging from short distances to almost global migrations, these birds can introduce zoonotic viruses, such as West Nile virus (WNV) or avian influenza virus (AIV), as well as unknown and potentially emerging viruses. Furthermore, they facilitate the global dispersal of infected ectoparasites, particularly ticks, risking the introduction of novel tick-borne diseases. To assess this risk, we sampled 42 bird species (39 migratory, 3 resident) over seven months in 2023 at the Bolle di Magadino nature reserve and the Piano di Magadino area in the canton Ticino (Switzerland). This region, because of its transitional climate, serves as an important resting and breeding ground for migratory birds. In total, 496 oropharyngeal-cloacal swabs, 164 sera, and 22 associated ticks were collected. papers.authors: Dušan Adamov, Milica Vranešević, Dragana Stamenov, Simonida Đurić
papers.abstract: Abstract Soil is a non-renewable natural resource essential for supporting plants, animals, and microorganisms. The intensification of conventional agriculture has substantially affected soil health, including its microbial component. This review evaluates how sustainable agricultural practices, including crop rotation, intercropping, cover cropping, organic amendments, and agroforestry, influence microbial aspects of soil health, with particular emphasis on microbial biomass, diversity, community composition, and functions related to nutrient cycling. Peer-reviewed studies published up to 2025 were identified through Web of Science, PubMed, and Google Scholar using combinations of terms describing individual agricultural practices and microbial soil health parameters. The reviewed evidence indicates that crop diversification can enhance microbial biomass and modify microbial community composition through changes in soil properties, nutrient cycling, root exudation, and organic inputs, although responses vary among cropping systems and environmental conditions. papers.abstract: Schrenk’s spruce ( Picea schrenkiana ) is a dominant coniferous tree species in the Western Tian Shan forests and plays an important ecological role in maintaining mountain forest ecosystems in Kyrgyzstan. In recent years, the Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve has seen a significant increase in diseased and declining spruce trees, raising concerns about forest health and ecosystem stability. The present study aimed to investigate the fungal communities associated with diseased roots, stems, and needles of Schrenk’s spruce in the Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve, Kyrgyzstan. We identified fungal isolates from symptomatic plant tissues using morphological characteristics, ITS (5.8S rRNA) sequencing, and species-specific molecular markers. Mycological analysis revealed a diverse fungal community associated with diseased spruce tissues. Penicillium and Talaromyces species were predominantly isolated from infected roots. papers.abstract: In the Global South, rapid urbanization intensifies pressures on natural resources, food security, and social equity, progressively displacing agriculture toward vulnerable peri-urban areas. Urban and peri-urban agriculture (UPA) has emerged as a strategic approach not only for food production but also for strengthening social cohesion, climate resilience, and territorial integration. Following the PRISMA protocol, a systematic literature review was conducted in the Scopus database (2017–2024) using Boolean operators related to UPA and Nexus frameworks. papers.title: Before Qualia, Strategic Existence Begins
papers.authors: Angelina Inesia-Forde
papers.abstract: Before evolution can select anything, a physically possible causal architecture must already exist for selection to exploit. The T4 bacteriophage, a mindless nanoscale machine whose structure executes functions that map onto both empowering and disempowering strategies in Forde's framework of social dynamics, demonstrates this principle at the nanoscale. The strategies mapped include security, knowledge, hope, fairness, unity, and dignity, alongside their darker counterparts: nativism, hierarchy, misinformation, subjugation, dehumanization, and fear. Each concept is paired with a specific biological mechanism, virion stability, irreversible adsorption, superinfection exclusion, among others, showing that the mapping is grounded in observable structure. These mappings do not reify nonhuman organisms or attribute human qualities to mindless machines. They are structural descriptions: the concepts name functions that the architecture performs, not feelings that the organism experiences. papers.abstract: Background: Adults with a modified lower urinary tract (MLUT) represent a growing but understudied population in renal transplantation. Concerns regarding long-term graft survival, infection, and urological morbidity persist, yet adult-specific outcome synthesis and clinically useful guidance are lacking. Methods: We performed a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses-compliant systematic review of studies reporting posttransplant outcomes in adults with abnormal or surgically MLUT anatomy. Primary outcomes were 1- and 5-y graft and patient survival. Secondary outcomes included urological complications. Given substantial heterogeneity, data were synthesized narratively. papers.authors: Camille Demassieux, Nicolas Rose, Guillaume Lhermie, Alexandre Hobeika, Stephen Valas
papers.abstract: Enzootic bovine leukosis (EBL), caused by the bovine leukemia virus (BLV), is a widespread bovine disease responsible for chronic economic losses in the cattle industry. Prevalence has risen substantially in countries without control measures, whereas state‑led programs have generated a more heterogeneous epidemiological landscape across Europe. This review examines key aspects of BLV impact and control in both global and European contexts. Using publicly available datasets from the World Organisation for Animal Health, it summarizes current BLV epidemiology and the outcomes of current control strategies. It also reviews emerging control options for high‑prevalence settings and challenges in economic assessment. Finally, it uses established findings from social science studies applied to veterinary public health to analyze issues linked to BLV control programs. The impact of BLV was greater than previously assumed, particularly in countries with high prevalence. papers.abstract: Automated tomato leaf disease classification remains challenging when different diseases exhibit similar color, texture, and necrotic symptoms. To improve pathological interpretability while maintaining competitive classification performance, this study proposes a multi-scale feature engineering framework that explicitly represents disease symptoms at both global and local scales. A composite Excess Green (ExG)-Triangle segmentation strategy is first used to preserve green, chlorotic, and diseased leaf tissues, achieving a Dice coefficient of 92.45% and a Recall of 99.40% on manually annotated leaf masks. A two-stage pruning strategy based on permutation importance and Pearson correlation reduces the feature dimensionality from 296 to 164, corresponding to a 44.6% reduction. The microbes most commonly isolated from poultry include Salmonella spp., Campylobacter jejuni , Campylobacter coli , Escherichia coli , Staphylococcus spp., and Listeria monocytogenes . A particular threat is posed by drug-resistant pathogens, which significantly limit the possibility of controlling infections and food contamination. papers.title: Characterization of two complete mitochondrial genomes of longhorn beetles (Coleoptera: Cerambycidae: Lepturinae) and their phylogenetic implications for the subfamily Lepturinae
papers.authors: Chaojie Wang, Bowen Tian, Meike Liu, Longyan Chen, Ping Wang
papers.abstract: Lepturinae is the third largest subfamily of the longhorn beetle family (Cerambycidae), however its phylogenetic relationships remain unclear. To address this, we sequenced and annotated the complete mitogenomes of Grammoptera (Neoencyclops) paucula and Encyclops hubeiensis, which were 16,095 bp and 16,448 bp in length, respectively. Each mitogenome contained 37 genes, including 13 protein-coding genes (PCGs), 22 transfer RNAs (tRNAs), two ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs), and a control region. Phylogenetic trees reconstructed from the 13 mitochondrial PCGs and their corresponding amino acid sequences datasets further clarified the evolutionary relationships within Lepturinae and resolved the phylogenetic relationships among its tribes.
